title: Where the depth goes: sort the candidates before you calculate
outcomes: Given three candidates, says which one gets the deep look and which get a short look
Gives the reason: a forcing line that keeps going, against a move whose piece can be taken for nothing or a quiet move
Tells a position that needs a deep look from a forced move and from a quiet one
Starts a time log that compares the seconds spent on critical and routine positions

steps.text: Depth is a budget you split between lines, not one number for the whole position. Sort the candidates first. **Deep look:** a forcing line (checks, captures, threats) with few replies, and it keeps going. **Short look:** a move whose piece can be taken for nothing (it is loose), or a quiet move that starts nothing. **No calculation:** only one legal move. A rule of thumb, not a tested method.

steps.caption: White to move. Candidates: A) Re8+  B) Qxg7+  C) Qe7. A gets the deep look: follow it to the end.

line.say: Re8+ is check, and the rook can be taken.

claims.statement: Re8+ forces checkmate in 3 or fewer against the engine's best defence (depth 16).

steps.caption: Same position. B) Qxg7+ gets a short look: follow it for two plies.

line.say: Qxg7+ takes a pawn, with check. But the queen on g7 is loose: nothing defends it.
Kxg7: the king takes the queen. White has given up a queen for a pawn.

claims.statement: After Qxg7+ the White pieces that are loose are exactly: e1, g7.
Qxg7+ is at least 4 pawns worse than the best move (depth 16).
After Qxg7+ the mover's net material change along the engine's best defence is at most -2 (depth 16).

steps.text: **When the sort fails.** It uses only what you can see: checks, captures, threats, and whether the moved piece can be taken free. A quiet move can hide the best line, so give quiet candidates a short look, not a pass. In an opening line you know, recall replaces calculation. Rule of thumb: stop deepening when the position is quiet or the result is forced, not when you are tired.

steps.title: Same line, one move later
steps.prompt: You just sorted the first position. The next is the same position after White's first move, and the last is an opening position. How much calculation does the player to move need? Predict, then check.
Say why the line you chose got the deep look. The answer is my judgement.

fields.label: It got the deep look because:
options: it is forcing and its piece cannot be taken for nothing
it is the first move I saw
it wins the most material at once
fields.answer: it is forcing and its piece cannot be taken for nothing

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** The next two exercises are silent. In each, you may decide that no candidate needs a deep look. The app shows no time log; the one below is yours, kept on paper or with a phone timer. Say first how many of the two you expect to get right.

steps.prompt: Commit to a number before the two silent exercises. This note stays on this device.

fields.label: I expect to get this many of the two right:

steps.text: Now spend the depth where it pays: two puzzles with the theme named, each a forced mate of four or five moves. Follow the forcing line to its end before you play.

**Time log: one session, on paper.** Take six positions from Practice (mixed). Before you solve each, write **C** (critical: a forcing line or a tempting capture) or **R** (routine: many moves about equal). Solve it with a timer running and write the seconds. Then average the seconds for C and for R. The aim: C takes longer than R. The app does not time this log.

steps.prompt: Plan one time-log session. A log of six positions is a rough first look, not a measurement. This note stays on this device.
